label: Quotient Manifolds
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 540 through 563 and asks a single sharp question: when is the orbit space of a smooth Lie group action again a smooth manifold? Frame the chapter as the search for two hypotheses, freeness and properness, that tame an otherwise wild quotient topology.

label: Group Actions, Orbits, Stabilizers
notes: Remind students that an action partitions the manifold into orbits, the level sets of the equivalence relation collapsed by the quotient map. The stabilizer measures how much of the group fixes a point. Emphasize that the orbit through a point is the image of the whole group acting on it.

label: The Orbit Space M/G
notes: Stress that the orbit space always exists as a topological space and that the quotient map is always open for a continuous action. The catch is that openness alone guarantees neither the Hausdorff property nor local Euclidean structure, which is exactly why naive quotients can fail.

label: When Quotients Go Wrong
notes: Walk through the gallery of failures. Rotation has a fixed origin that becomes a singular endpoint class; the full linear action glues all nonzero vectors into one orbit producing a non-Hausdorff two-point quotient. Each failed hypothesis leaves a visible geometric scar in the orbit space.

label: Free Actions
notes: Define freeness as triviality of every stabilizer: only the identity can fix any point. Explain the dimensional payoff, that a free action makes every orbit an immersed copy of the group, so orbits all share the dimension of G. Freeness controls isotropy but says nothing yet about topology.

label: Proper Actions
notes: Introduce properness through the action map sending a pair to the moved point and the original point; the action is proper when this map is proper, meaning preimages of compact sets are compact. Give the sequence test as the working criterion students will actually apply in examples.

label: Properness Stops Escape
notes: Use the dilation example to make properness concrete. Take points one over i and group elements i; both the points and their images converge to zero, yet the group elements escape to infinity. This failure of properness is exactly what lets a non-Hausdorff quotient sneak in.

label: Free Is Not Proper
notes: The irrational torus flow is the cautionary tale: it is free because no nonzero time returns a point to itself, yet every orbit is dense. The only saturated open sets are empty or everything, so the quotient cannot separate points. Free without proper is not enough.

label: The Quotient Manifold Theorem
notes: State the central theorem carefully. A smooth, free, and proper Lie group action yields an orbit space that is a topological manifold with a unique smooth structure making the quotient map a smooth submersion. Underline the uniqueness clause, which makes the smooth structure canonical rather than a choice.

label: Adapted Charts
notes: Sketch the proof engine. Properness shrinks a transverse slice so each orbit meets it once; freeness keeps the limiting group element from fixing the base. In the resulting adapted chart the quotient map reads as projection onto the slice coordinates, giving rank equal to dim M minus dim G.

label: Descending Maps to the Quotient
notes: Explain the characteristic property of submersions: a map out of M that is constant on orbits descends to a unique smooth map on the quotient. This is the everyday tool that lets us define smooth functions and maps on orbit spaces without building charts by hand each time.

label: Homogeneous Spaces G/H
notes: Show that a transitive action realizes a manifold as cosets of the isotropy subgroup of a base point. The sphere as SO(n+1) over SO(n) is the model: spinning the frame about the north pole changes the matrix but not its image, so the quotient forgets exactly the isotropy directions.

label: Coverings and Lie Quotients
notes: Close by collecting applications. Discrete free proper actions make quotient maps into normal covering maps, with the lattice quotient of the plane giving the torus. The line over the integers gives the circle, and closed normal subgroups yield quotient Lie groups, all from one mechanism.
